kf: **Drug photosensitivity** is a rash on sun-exposed skin caused by a drug plus UV (mostly UVA).
Common culprits: tetracyclines (doxycycline), thiazides, amiodarone, voriconazole, NSAIDs, quinolones, phenothiazines.
Sharp cut-off at clothing lines; spares under the chin, behind the ears and skin folds.
Stop or switch the culprit with the prescriber (never stop amiodarone, voriconazole or antiretrovirals without specialist input); strict UVA protection.

sub: Common in older people on multiple drugs; holiday or summer onset.

aet: Photosensitising drug in the skin plus UVA (passes through window glass).
myths: **"Sunscreen fixes it"**: many sunscreens protect poorly against UVA; clothing and avoiding sun matter.
patho_lead: A drug in the skin **absorbs UV energy** and damages cells directly or creates an allergen.

mech.t: The drug or its metabolite reaches the dermis and epidermis.
Absorbed UVA excites the drug, releasing free radicals that damage cells: sunburn-like reaction within hours.
UV converts the drug into a hapten; T cells become sensitised: eczema days later, may spread beyond exposed sites.
Some drugs (amiodarone, minocycline) leave slate-grey or blue pigment in exposed skin.

histo: Phototoxic: necrotic keratinocytes like sunburn. Photoallergic: spongiotic dermatitis. Phototesting confirms in specialist units.

sub: Tetracyclines and psoralens can lift the nails from the bed after sun exposure.

comp: Blistering, pigmentation, persistent light reaction (chronic actinic dermatitis).
prog: Phototoxic reactions clear when the drug stops (amiodarone may take months); photoallergy can persist.
